title: Logical Connectives
tagline: Year 2 — And, or, if-then, only if, unless, negation and valid inferences

introduction.overview: Logical connectives are the small words that join statements: and, or, if…then, only if, unless and not. Their meaning is exact. "P and Q" is true only when both are true. "P or Q" is true when at least one is true. "If P then Q" is false only when P is true and Q is false. Understanding these meanings lets you negate statements correctly and draw valid conclusions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Questions on connectives, negations and conditional statements are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds, in the form of "which of the following follows" or "which is the negation".
introduction.realWorldContext: Programming conditions, legal clauses and search queries (AND, OR, NOT) all follow these rules.

learningObjectives: Know the truth conditions of and, or, if-then, only-if and unless
Form the negation of compound statements (De Morgan's laws)
Write the converse and contrapositive of a conditional
Draw valid inferences (modus ponens, modus tollens, chain)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A statement is true or false. The negation of a true statement is false and vice versa.

coreDefinitions: Conjunction "P and Q": true only if both are true. Disjunction "P or Q": true if at least one is true (inclusive).
Conditional "If P then Q": false only when P is true and Q is false. P is the antecedent and Q the consequent.
Converse: If Q then P. Contrapositive: If not Q then not P. A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, not to its converse.
"P only if Q" means "If P then Q". "Unless P, Q" means "If not P, then Q".
De Morgan's laws: not (P and Q) = (not P) or (not Q); not (P or Q) = (not P) and (not Q).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A conditional is a promise: "If it rains, the match is cancelled." The promise is broken only when it rains and the match is not cancelled. If it does not rain, the promise says nothing. This is why the converse is not equivalent.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Rewrite every statement in the form "if … then …". Then use the contrapositive for reverse reasoning and the chain rule for two conditionals.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Negation of and/or
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: not (P and Q) = not P or not Q;  not (P or Q) = not P and not Q
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Not (raining and cold) = not raining or not cold

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Negation of quantifiers
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: not (All A are B) = Some A are not B;  not (Some A are B) = No A is B
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Not all birds fly = some birds do not fly

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Conditional forms
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If P then Q ≡ If not Q then not P;  not equivalent to If Q then P
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Contrapositive of "if even then x² even"

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Only if and unless
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: P only if Q ≡ If P then Q;  Unless P, Q ≡ If not P then Q
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Unless you study, you fail = if you do not study, you fail

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Valid inferences
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: P→Q, P ⊢ Q (modus ponens);  P→Q, not Q ⊢ not P (modus tollens);  P→Q, Q→R ⊢ P→R
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Rain → cancelled; not cancelled → no rain

mainNarrative: Start by understanding when each compound statement is true. "P and Q" requires both. "P or Q" is true if at least one is true. "If P then Q" is false only if P is true and Q is false; in particular a false antecedent makes it true, so "If 2 + 2 = 5, then the moon is made of cheese" is true.

To negate a compound statement, use De Morgan's laws. The negation of "It is raining and cold" is "It is not raining or it is not cold". The negation of "All birds fly" is "Some birds do not fly", and the negation of "Some students are absent" is "No student is absent".

For conditionals, the contrapositive is equivalent to the original: "If x is even then x² is even" has the contrapositive "If x² is not even then x is not even". The converse ("If x² is even then x is even") may or may not be true and must be checked separately.
Translate special words. "I will go only if it does not rain" means "If I go, it does not rain". "Unless you study, you will fail" means "If you do not study, you will fail".

Valid inferences: from "If it rains the match is cancelled" and "It rained" conclude it was cancelled; from the same statement and "It was not cancelled" conclude it did not rain. From "If the ground is wet it rained" the fact that the ground is wet does not prove it rained: that is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

deepDiveAspects.title: Inclusive and exclusive or
deepDiveAspects.content: In logic, "or" is inclusive: both may be true. "Either P or Q but not both" is exclusive.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why a false antecedent makes a conditional true
deepDiveAspects.content: The promise "if P then Q" has not been broken if P did not happen. So it counts as true by default.

solvedExamples.title: De Morgan
solvedExamples.question: What is the negation of "It is raining and it is cold"?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: not (P and Q) = not P or not Q.

steps.title: Apply the law
steps.explanation: Negate each part and change and to or.

steps.title: Result
steps.explanation: It is not raining or it is not cold.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It is not raining or it is not cold
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The original fails if either part fails.

solvedExamples.title: Contrapositive
solvedExamples.question: Every day it rains the match is cancelled. The match was not cancelled. What follows?

steps.title: Contrapositive
steps.explanation: If not cancelled, then no rain.

steps.title: Apply
steps.explanation: The match was not cancelled, so it did not rain.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive.

solvedExamples.title: Only if and unless
solvedExamples.question: Rewrite "I will go only if it does not rain" and "Unless you study, you will fail" as if-then statements.

steps.title: Only if
steps.explanation: "P only if Q" means If P then Q: If I go, then it does not rain.

steps.title: Unless
steps.explanation: "Unless P, Q" means If not P then Q: If you do not study, you will fail.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: If I go, it does not rain; if you do not study, you will fail
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The connective words have exact meanings.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Reversing the direction of only if.

shortcutMethods.title: Translate and contrapose

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Rewrite as if-then, use the contrapositive to reason backwards, and apply De Morgan to negations.

rulesForApplication: Never swap the direction of a conditional.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating "if Q then P" as equivalent.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject answers that use the converse or affirm the consequent.

easy.question: The negation of "It is raining and it is cold" is
options: It is not raining and it is not cold
It is not raining or it is not cold
It is raining or it is cold
It is raining and it is not cold
easy.correctAnswer: It is not raining or it is not cold
easy.explanation: By De Morgan's law: not (P and Q) = not P or not Q.

easy.question: The negation of "All birds can fly" is
options: Some birds cannot fly
No bird can fly
All birds cannot fly
Some birds can fly

easy.question: If P then Q is true and P is true. Then
options: Q is false
Nothing can be said about Q
P is false
Q is true
easy.explanation: Modus ponens: from P → Q and P we get Q.

intermediate.question: The contrapositive of "If x is even, then x² is even" is
options: If x² is not even, then x is not even
If x² is even, then x is even
If x is not even, then x² is not even
If x is even, then x² is not even
intermediate.correctAnswer: If x² is not even, then x is not even
intermediate.explanation: Contrapositive: If not Q then not P.

intermediate.question: "I will go only if it does not rain" means
options: If it does not rain, I will go
If I do not go, it rains
I will go if it rains
If I go, then it does not rain
intermediate.correctAnswer: If I go, then it does not rain
intermediate.explanation: "P only if Q" means If P then Q.

intermediate.question: "Unless you study, you will fail" is equivalent to
options: If you study, you will fail
If you fail, you did not study
If you study, you will pass
If you do not study, you will fail
intermediate.correctAnswer: If you do not study, you will fail
intermediate.explanation: "Unless P, Q" means If not P then Q.

advanced.question: If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore it rained. This reasoning is
options: valid (modus ponens)
valid (modus tollens)
invalid (affirming the consequent)
valid (contrapositive)
advanced.explanation: The ground may be wet for another reason. Q does not imply P.

advanced.question: The negation of "If P then Q" is
options: not P and Q
P and not Q
not P or Q
If not P then not Q
advanced.explanation: A conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false.

placementStyle.question: A is true only if B is true. B is false. Then
options: A is true
A is false
A may be true or false
B is true
placementStyle.explanation: A → B and not B give not A.

placementStyle.question: "Neither Ravi nor Meena passed" means
options: Ravi did not pass and Meena did not pass
Ravi did not pass or Meena did not pass
Ravi passed or Meena passed
Only one of them passed
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Ravi did not pass and Meena did not pass

placementStyle.question: All who study pass. Anil did not pass. Therefore
options: Anil studied
Anil may have studied
Everyone who did not study failed
Anil did not study
placementStyle.explanation: Contrapositive: if not pass, then not study.

quickFormulas: not(P and Q) = not P or not Q

selfCheckQuestions: Can I spot affirming the consequent?
